summary: First lit November 15, 1855 on Point Loma, San Diego. Lit until 1891, when the light moved to a new tower lower on the point. Now a restored museum in Cabrillo National Monument.

lens.where: lantern room; LighthouseFriends says the third-order lens there came from Mile Rocks Light

structures.note: Restored; NPS says the interior is refurbished to its 1880s appearance.

access.note: Part of Cabrillo National Monument. Open daily 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM (NPS). Tower climbed only on special Open Tower Days; not wheelchair accessible.

visit.note: Tower open only on special Open Tower Days (NPS).

events.note: Completed by the end of August 1854; first lighting delayed until November 1855 by the lens (LighthouseFriends).
Lit November 15, 1855, with a third-order Fresnel lens.
Third-order Fresnel lens installed November 1855.
Severe gale on October 2, 1858 for six hours; ships dragged anchor; the keeper left the tower at noon.
Earthquake damaged the lighthouse, four years after the 1858 gale; extent not known (NPS).
Large concrete catch basin added in front of the lighthouse (NPS 1883; LighthouseFriends 1882).
Tower painted white, the first time it was not left sandstone colour (cement-coated walls painted from 1879 onward).
Changed on April 1, 1889 to fixed white varied by red and white flashes, one-minute interval; a rotating red shield probably made the flashes (NPS).
Light extinguished March 23, 1891, when the new light was first exhibited; the old tower was abandoned.
Light moved to a new iron skeleton tower on the tip of the point, 88 feet above the sea.
After abandonment the building was vandalized: windows broken, pieces carried off (NPS, NRHP).

Presidential Proclamation dated October 10, 1913 set aside one-half acre as Cabrillo National Monument; Order of Panama proposed a 150-foot Cabrillo statue, never built. Dedication ceremonies held September 26, 1913.
Army spent $360 repairing the old building.
Ninth Army Corps renovated the building; Lighthouse Service Bulletin says it is preserved as a memorial and was repaired and painted.
Monument transferred to the National Park Service under the 1933 reorganisation.
Restoration of the building completed; concessioner set up a tearoom.
Visits stopped for wartime security; Navy used the lighthouse as a signal tower for harbor entry.
Public welcomed back on November 11, 1946.
On the 100th anniversary, 15 November 1955, the tower was lit by an electric bulb for show only.
Added to the National Register of Historic Places (LighthouseFriends).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 141 m is the light's height above the water: NPS says the lens stood 462 feet (141 m) above the water. NPS also gives 422 feet (129 m) for the tower's site above the bay entrance. The 1931 Bulletin gives 462 feet as the light's height above the sea. The two figures are different measures, not a conflict.

NPS calls David Splaine the first keeper of Ballast Point. The USLHS roster names John M. Nilsson as head keeper from 1890 to 1892 and Splaine from 1895 to 1916. Both are shown; the story does not pick one.

notes_for_editor: (1) Sources are strong: the NRHP nomination's statement of significance was read in full (the cache has the whole form); the NPS history (sections 2 and 3) was read in full; NPS grounds and visitor pages; the 1931 Bulletin and the 1891 Light-House Board report were read at the page. (2) The Light-House Board 1891 page is scan page 211; its printed page is not confirmed by the OCR header and is not cited. (3) Dates of the catch basin differ: NPS says 1883 (the story gives the NPS date and LighthouseFriends' 1882). (4) Old light height: NPS grounds page says 422 feet above the bay entrance and 462 feet for the lens above the water; the 1931 Bulletin says 462 feet above the sea; NPS also prints an 1874 newspaper figure of 480 feet and brackets it as 462 feet. (5) The 1869 Gatewood visit comes from the San Diego Union through LighthouseFriends, as quoted; the paper itself was not found in Chronicling America (no 1869 hit). (6) The roster's keeper lines are matched to the USLHS place by name and position (0.43 km); they are USLHS/NARA-derived and are not confirmed in primary registers here. The keepers Keating, Israel, Jenkins, Tolman and Splaine are also named in the NPS history. Eliza Jenkins's relation to John D. Jenkins is not stated in any source read. The NPS history says the first keeper operated San Diego's first shipyard but does not name him there; the story now states that the link to Keating is an inference from the NPS's 1855 and 1858 references to 'the keeper' and 'Capt. Keating', and no source connects them directly. (7) The NPS history says the first keeper ran a shipyard but does not name him there; the story links that to Keating only through the 1858 account and the roster order, and says so. (8) Ballast Point: NPS calls David Splaine that station's first keeper; the USLHS roster has John M. Nilsson first (1890-1892) and Splaine 1895-1916. (9) The 1925 Lighthouse Service Bulletin names a second assistant keeper 'of Point Loma Lighthouse'. That is the active light at the tip, not the old tower, so it is not in this roster. (10) What became of the 1855 lens is not stated in the sources read; LighthouseFriends says the lantern now holds a third-order lens from Mile Rocks Light. (11) The NRHP form's entry-date stamp is illegible in the OCR; the listing year 1974 is from LighthouseFriends. (12) Fixes in the fact-check pass: the 1946 public welcome is now placed before the 1947 inspection; the 1931 Bulletin's '462 feet' and '88 feet' are read as heights above the sea, as the Bulletin prints them; the Bulletin's fog statement is cited to its own page. (13) Mary Israel's knitting is an NPS 'some say' and is now marked as hearsay. (14) The story now uses the nomination's wording 'first successful effort' and 'newly acquired west coast' as unquoted paraphrase, sourced to the NRHP nomination (the draft had 'first effort' and 'new west coast'). The Bulletin's fog sentence is OCR-garbled in one word (obsClu·ed), so only 'by high fogs' is quoted.
